title: Parallel organum at the fourth (constructed example)
desc: An illustration written for the Atlas of Musical Style, not taken from a source: the principal voice (Cantus) sings a plain melody and the organal voice (Tenor) follows it throughout a perfect fourth below, as Musica enchiriadis (c. 870) describes. The melody avoids B so that no tritone arises. The treatise writes it in unmeasured daseian signs; here every note has the same length.

title: Free organum with occursus (constructed example)
desc: An illustration written for the Atlas of Musical Style, not taken from a source: the organal voice (Tenor) begins on the unison, moves obliquely and in parallel to the fourth, and returns to the unison by a second (the occursus), as Guido of Arezzo teaches in the Micrologus (c. 1026). Thirds and seconds are allowed beside the fourth. Every note has the same length here.

title: Fauxbourdon (constructed example)
desc: An illustration written for the Atlas of Musical Style, not taken from a source: the Cantus is a plain tune; the Tenor runs a sixth below it and the middle voice, the fauxbourdon itself, a fourth below the Cantus, so every chord is a triad in first inversion. At the cadence the sixth opens to the octave: Cantus and middle voice rise a step, the Tenor falls a step. A fauxbourdon was written as Cantus and Tenor only; the middle voice was sung by ear.
